note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: text is printable ASCII (codes 32 to 126) with at least one non-space character
clarifyingQuestions: Can text contain several spaces in a row, or leading and trailing spaces?
Is an over-long word allowed only alone on its line?
Does the width count the separating spaces?
hints: Placing as many words as possible on each line never increases the number of lines.
Track the length of the current line; adding a word costs one space plus its length.
If the word does not fit (or the line is empty), start a new line with that word; an over-long word therefore always gets a line to itself.
invariants: the current line length never exceeds maxWidth unless the line holds one over-long word
the line count is non-decreasing over the scan
chooseWhen: Minimum wrapped-line counts with uniform separators
tradeoffs: The greedy rule is optimal for counting lines but not for balanced (pretty) wrapping, which needs dynamic programming
hack2hire:68757267ab23078e4e46aa3c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: minimum number of greedy-wrapped lines

constraints: each trade matches the four-field format
clarifyingQuestions: What is returned: the unmatched trades, the matched pairs, or counts?
In which order are unmatched trades listed?
When several trades could match, which pair is chosen?
Is there a further matching rule (for example house buys offsetting house sells)?
hints: Identical strings are interchangeable, so only their counts matter.
Count the street trades by string; each house trade consumes one count of its own string if available.
Unconsumed house trades and remaining street counts are the unmatched trades; sort the combined list.
invariants: every matched pair has identical strings
the number of unmatched trades has the parity of h + s
chooseWhen: Reconciling two ledgers of identical records
tradeoffs: A sort-and-merge pass needs no hash map but sorts both lists first
hack2hire:67eb34914c9bb801bfd0ef7d.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: exact one-to-one trade matching

constraints: each trade matches the four-field format
clarifyingQuestions: What is returned: the unmatched trades, the matched pairs, or counts?
In which order are unmatched trades listed?
When several trades could match, which pair is chosen?
Is there a further matching rule (for example house buys offsetting house sells)?
hints: Run the exact round first; it is the same multiset matching as level 1.
Group the leftovers by everything except the ID (the first three comma-separated fields).
Within a group, sort both sides and pair positions 0..min-1; the rest of the larger side stays unmatched.
invariants: exact matches are never broken by the second round
within a group at most one side has leftovers
chooseWhen: Reconciliation with a fallback looser key
tradeoffs: Matching rules applied in rounds are easy to extend; a single weighted matching would be more general but costlier
hack2hire:67eb3ff94c9bb801bfd0ef7e.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: exact matching, then attribute matching ignoring the ID

clarifyingQuestions: What fills a cell whose code has no record at that timestamp?
Are records with an unknown code an error or ignored?
Can the stream arrive out of timestamp order?
Is the timestamp part of the row?
hints: Sort the registered codes once so each code has a fixed column.
Group the records by timestamp, keeping arrival order inside a group.
Sweep timestamps in increasing order with one current-value array: apply the group, then copy the array (with the timestamp in front) as the row.
invariants: every row has 1 + codes.length cells
a cell is null only before the first record of its code
chooseWhen: Pivoting sparse event streams into dense snapshots
tradeoffs: Copying the full row per timestamp costs O(c) each; storing only changes is smaller but harder to read
hack2hire:69cd7029ff3ebde766cee760.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: carry-forward matrix rows per timestamp

clarifyingQuestions: Is the text of the token chunk before "<END>" kept, and is it kept when empty?
What if no stop token appears?
Which occurrence counts when "<END>" appears more than once?
Can the token span several chunks?
hints: Because the token is inside one chunk, each chunk can be searched on its own.
Copy chunks to the output until one contains "<END>".
From that chunk keep only the text before the token, and only when it is non-empty; then stop.
invariants: output length <= input length
every output chunk except possibly the last is an unchanged input chunk
chooseWhen: Cutting model output at a sentinel while preserving chunk boundaries
tradeoffs: Searching chunk by chunk is simplest but misses tokens split across chunks, which level 2 handles
hack2hire:6a5019e9665efda9311f5903.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: truncate at a stop token inside one chunk

clarifyingQuestions: Is the text of the token chunk before "<END>" kept, and is it kept when empty?
What if no stop token appears?
Which occurrence counts when "<END>" appears more than once?
Can the token span several chunks?
hints: Per-chunk search fails when "<E" ends one chunk and "ND>" starts the next.
Search the concatenation (or carry the last four characters of the previous text) to find where the token starts.
Convert that start offset to (chunk index, offset) by walking the chunk lengths; keep earlier chunks and the non-empty prefix of that chunk.
invariants: the token start offset is the first in the concatenation
no output text overlaps the token
chooseWhen: Sentinel detection in streams split at arbitrary boundaries
tradeoffs: Joining costs O(total) memory; a rolling four-character carry would stream with O(1) extra memory
hack2hire:6a501a01665efda9311f5906.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: truncate at a stop token that may span chunks

constraints: matrix and s use lowercase letters
clarifyingQuestions: What is the third direction?
Is a one-character string counted once per direction?
Do overlapping occurrences count separately?
hints: Each direction turns the matrix into independent lines: rows, columns and diagonals.
A match from (cell, direction) is an occurrence of s starting at that cell on its line.
Count overlapping occurrences per line with a prefix-function (KMP) scan, so long repetitive lines stay linear.
invariants: every cell belongs to exactly one line per direction
occurrences are counted at their starting index, so overlaps all count
chooseWhen: Word search along fixed directions
tradeoffs: Naive comparison is O(m n |s|); KMP is linear but needs the failure table
hack2hire:6a14eb4e7b0582b35278812d.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: count right, down and diagonal occurrences

clarifyingQuestions: Is any valid rearrangement accepted, or a particular one?
What is returned when no arrangement exists?
Should all arrangements be listed?
hints: An arrangement exists iff the most frequent letter appears at most ceil(n / 2) times.
Build the answer left to right, always trying the smallest letter that differs from the previous one.
A choice c is safe iff the rest (r letters) has max count <= ceil(r / 2) and, when r is odd and some letter needs every even slot, that letter is not c.
invariants: the prefix built so far never has equal neighbours
after each step the remaining multiset stays arrangeable after the last letter
chooseWhen: Canonical answers for problems with many valid outputs
tradeoffs: Lexicographic greed needs a precise feasibility test; any-valid answers can use a simpler max-heap
hack2hire:6887e0fc6509c24ee64e4b21.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: lexicographically smallest valid rearrangement

constraints: plans has exactly 3 entries, names match [A-Za-z]{1,10}
years between 1900 and 2100 (leap years per the Gregorian rule)
clarifyingQuestions: What exactly is returned: a total, per-month totals or a per-day log?
Is the END day itself billed?
How is a fractional amount rounded?
Does an active plan bill through the end of the year?
hints: Within one month every day has the same divisor N, so the month total is (sum of price * days) / N.
Convert dates to day-of-year; consecutive events bound intervals with one plan (or none).
Split each interval by month lengths (February has 29 days in leap years), add price * days to the month numerator, and round numerator / N half up with integers.
invariants: each billed day belongs to exactly one interval
numerators are integers; only the final division rounds
chooseWhen: Prorated billing that must stay exact
tradeoffs: Day-by-day simulation is simpler but O(365); interval splitting scales to long histories
hack2hire:68c331ec1f64f4312b0a3e2d.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: monthly prorated statement in cents

clarifyingQuestions: Are values distinct?
Is target 0 reachable with the empty subset?
Can target exceed the total?
hints: Track the set of sums reachable with the elements seen so far; it starts as {0}.
Adding element x makes every old sum s also reachable as s + x.
Store the set as bits of one integer: reach |= reach << x, keeping only bits up to target; answer whether bit target is set.
invariants: bit 0 is always set
the bitset never holds sums above target
chooseWhen: Pseudo-polynomial decision problems with small targets
tradeoffs: A bitset is fast but O(target) memory; meet-in-the-middle suits few elements with huge values

clarifyingQuestions: Is an empty filter matched by every group?
Can a tag repeat in a group?
Must the output be in a particular order?
hints: A hash set of each group answers "contains every filter tag" in O(|filter|).
Skip groups that miss any filter tag.
Collect the remaining tags of valid groups in a set, drop filter tags, then sort for a canonical answer.
invariants: result tags are distinct and never in filter
each result tag occurs in some valid group
chooseWhen: Faceted tag search and co-occurrence queries
tradeoffs: An inverted index from tag to groups helps with many queries; one query needs only a scan
hack2hire:696a84b7cc483345efb1b23c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: tags co-occurring with every filter tag

clarifyingQuestions: Is the input one string or a list of lines?
Is a final line without newline counted?
What does n = 0 return?
Should a missing final newline be added?
hints: A line starts at index 0 and after every "\n" that is not the last character.
Keep only the most recent n line starts in a ring buffer (a queue of size n).
After the scan, return the suffix from the oldest start still in the buffer, or "" when n is 0.
invariants: the buffer never holds more than n starts
the result is always a suffix of text
chooseWhen: Streaming last-k retention
tradeoffs: Scanning backward for n newlines is faster on large files with random access; the ring buffer works on a forward-only stream
hack2hire:677c6cdc5cbaff553b53b06c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: last n lines of a text, tail -n semantics

constraints: plural values are decimal integers 0 to 1e6 without leading zeros
clarifyingQuestions: Which branch does 0 use?
Is "#" replaced in both branches?
What happens to an unknown name?
Can placeholders nest inside plural branches?
hints: Put keys and values into a hash map.
Scan the text; at "{" read the name up to "}" or ",".
For a plural block, read the two branch texts between the fixed delimiters, choose by value == "1", and replace "#" with the value; copy unknown expressions unchanged.
invariants: literal text is copied byte for byte
every expression is consumed exactly once
chooseWhen: Message formatting with simple pluralisation
tradeoffs: A hand-written parser is linear and precise; regular expressions are shorter but harder to extend to nesting
hack2hire:69d18cb017b72775cc49c0c4.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: placeholders and ICU-style plural blocks

clarifyingQuestions: Is the returned word lowercased?
Is each pair a string or a [word, count] list?
How are ties ordered?
For the stream version, can a word span two added texts?
hints: Scan characters, building a lowercase word while letters continue and counting it when a non-letter ends it.

clarifyingQuestions: Do queries return ids only or ids with totals?
How are ties broken?
Can quantity be zero or negative (returns)?
What if k exceeds the number of books?
hints: Store each total in a hash map so a sale updates it in O(1).
Keep all books in one array ordered by (-total, id); totals only grow, so a book only moves toward the front.
Locate the old key and the new slot with binary search, splice the book, and answer getTopK with a slice.

map keys and array entries are the same set of books

Are duplicates kept?
Can k be 0 or exceed the length?
hints: Only the k largest values matter; keep them in a min-heap whose root is the smallest kept value.
For each new value larger than the root, replace the root and sift down.
Sort the k kept values decreasingly for a canonical answer.

the root is the k-th largest so far

tradeoffs: Quickselect is O(n) average but reorders a copy; a heap streams in O(n log k)

clarifyingQuestions: Can a pin id be added twice (update)?
How are equal scores ordered?
What does an unknown type return?
Are ids or whole pins returned?
hints: Pins of different types never compete, so keep one structure per type.
Keep each type's pins sorted by (-score, id); insertion uses binary search.
